AI-assisted individuals match unassisted teams on solution quality and produce proposals that integrate technical and commercial perspectives more evenly. The research also records improved self-reported emotions. These results concern consumer-product innovation; applying them to software teams requires a separate inference.
attributes.limitation: Product-innovation work in one consumer-goods firm; implications for software teams require an explicit domain transfer.

records.label: Automating Feature Flag Cleanup at Scale with Multi-Agent LLM Systems: An Industrial Experience at DoorDash
records.summary: A DoorDash system combines live feature-flag configuration, issue tracking, isolated code edits and validation to propose removal of stale flags. In an evaluation of 50 flags, 45 resulting pull requests were approved; mean agent runtime was 13.8 minutes and mean agent cost was $4.79. This single-company experience supports a bounded maintenance workflow, while agent runtime excludes some human effort and is not a controlled estimate of time saved.
records.limitation: Single-company maintenance case with 50 flags; agent runtime and API cost omit some human work and do not establish causal savings.

records.label: On the Risks of using LLM-Generated Tests for Regression Testing
records.summary: An experiment uses 145 real pull requests from SciPy, Qiskit and pandas with injected faults to study generated regression tests. Tests more often encode faulty behavior as expected output than expose it, and many faulty expectations persist across subsequent revisions. The findings identify an oracle problem: executable tests can preserve a defect. Results depend on one model and synthetic mutations rather than the prevalence of production faults.
records.limitation: Injected mutations and one model; generated tests that pass can preserve faulty behavior rather than specify correctness.

records.label: Security Impact of Coding Agent’s Memory Files
records.summary: An exploratory experiment adds malicious repository memory instructions to 36 C/C++ security tasks. records.label: On the Reliability of LLM-Based Vulnerability Patching Benchmarks
records.summary: A vulnerability-patching benchmark assembles 112 historical bugs from 84 repositories and evaluates repairs using proof-of-concept attacks, regression tests and developer-intent tests. Benchmark infrastructure, instructions, permissions, leaked solutions and incomplete correctness checks can each distort agent scores. Successful attack suppression need not satisfy the developer-intent checks, so a single pass rate is insufficient evidence of a reliable security repair.
records.limitation: Scores depend on information, harness behavior and the selected oracles; attack suppression alone does not show an upstream-quality repair.

records.label: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
records.summary: Snapshots of 50 long-lived Java and Python projects compare similarity, static-analysis quality and evolution before widespread LLM assistance and during later development. The study finds no consistent homogenization signal; Java similarity falls on some measures and Python differences are not significant. The observational era comparison cannot by itself attribute changes to AI adoption.
records.limitation: Era comparisons and traced tool use do not randomize adoption; static-analysis changes cannot be attributed directly to AI.

records.label: Testing with Coding Agents: A Large-Scale Comparison of Agent-Supported and Human-Authored Pull Requests
records.summary: An observational comparison covers 114,134 merged pull requests in 391 Java repositories. After accounting for repository and change size, agent-supported changes are more likely to touch tests, particularly by adding them; pooled rates are nearly equal. Coverage of production changes shows no detected difference. These findings describe test-editing behavior, not a demonstrated improvement in test quality or defect prevention.
records.limitation: Observational merged-PR sample; editing or adding tests does not establish test quality, defect prevention or causality.

records.label: Not All Correct Fixes Run Alike: An Empirical Study of Patch Performance in Repository-Level Issue Resolution
records.summary: Researchers compare distinct patches that all pass the same issue-resolution tests. Among 262 Python benchmark issues with multiple correct fixes, 41.98% show significant instruction-count differences and 34.73% show elapsed-time differences. Models ranked highly for resolving issues are not necessarily ranked highly for efficient patches. The selected regression tests provide a constrained runtime workload rather than comprehensive application-performance validation.
records.limitation: Selected Python issues and regression-test workloads; runtime differences are workload-specific, not a complete production performance assessment.

records.label: Who Pays the Review Cost? Triage, Fairness, and Accountability in AI-authored Pull Requests
records.summary: A survey of 239 practitioners in 31 countries examines how reviewers triage AI-authored pull requests. Respondents place value on explained intent, bounded scope, tests and an identifiable human owner, and report reluctance to accept AI changes solely because continuous integration passes. The study describes missing rationale, validation and ownership as reviewability debt. Its evidence is stated attitudes and reported experience, not directly observed review outcomes.
records.limitation: Survey scenarios and self-reports, not observed acceptance or review-time measurements; respondents are not a random global developer sample.

records.label: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
records.summary: An analysis of 496 LLM call sites in 40 open-source agentic systems compares expected behavioral constraints with implemented checks. Although 82% have checks before and after the call, only 5.3% of judged sites enforce their full expected contract. Runtime experiments reproduce 38 gap mechanisms and stop them by enforcing missing constraints. The result concerns the adequacy of checks against reconstructed contracts, rather than their mere presence.
records.limitation: Expected contracts are reconstructed and human-judged; inspect the rubric and denominator before generalizing the complete-contract percentage.

records.label: The Vanishing Advantage of Specialization: AI, Knowledge Utilization, and the Boundary of the Firm
records.summary: An economic model explains how cheaper access to specialist knowledge can shift recurring work inside client firms while leaving rare problems with outside specialists. Descriptive occupational data are consistent with that mechanism: software developers' employment share in their main specialist industry fell from 34.3% in 2022 to 30.5% in 2025. The evidence does not identify AI as the cause.
records.limitation: A theoretical mechanism with descriptive supporting patterns; occupational trends do not identify AI's causal employment effect.

records.label: The Customer Is the Builder: How AI Coding Agents Are Rewriting the Economics of Software
records.summary: The paper separates software-building capability, adoption and substitution for purchased software. Its evidence combines reproducible public-data analysis and an illustrative public software-building case, open-source alternatives, surveys and aggregate investment indicators. It argues that customers can increasingly build tools themselves, while acknowledging that actual purchasing displacement remains weakly identified. Candidate alternatives and successful builds are capacity signals; they do not measure realized market replacement, and the paper’s forecasts are extrapolations.
records.limitation: Mixed capability demonstrations and descriptive market evidence; candidate alternatives and forecasts are not observed purchasing substitution.

records.label: Engineering Requirements for Generative AI Agents: The BARD Process Theory
records.summary: Grounded-theory analysis of 36 practitioner interviews develops BARD, a process account of requirements work for generative-AI agents. The qualitative model explains reported practice and proposes a framework; it does not establish that the process is universally applicable or causally superior.

records.limitation: Controlled skill-conflict probes and repository sampling; task success alone does not measure fidelity to the intended skill.

records.label: Your Wish Is My Commit: Over-Compliant Refactoring in AI Coding Agents
records.summary: Repeated open-ended refactoring requests test whether coding agents stop when an already-clean codebase needs no further change. Across 3,000 turns, all tested models continue making edits, sometimes after declaring completion. The experiment motivates explicit stopping criteria and measures of unnecessary churn; it does not establish the frequency of this behavior in ordinary development.
records.limitation: Repeated open-ended refactoring is a deliberate stress test, not an estimate of unnecessary changes in ordinary work.
